How move counting works in matching games

When NoCharge Memory Match counts a two-card attempt, why mismatches still count, and why the move total is not saved as a V2 best score.

By NoCharge·Reviewed by NoCharge·Published August 15, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Try the detail in a live board.

Flip cards. Find pairs.

Play Memory MatchBrowse all Articles

Bottom line: In Memory Match, one move is one two-card attempt. The counter increases when the second different card is revealed, whether the pair matches or not.

The current board has sixteen cards arranged as eight symbol pairs. The first reveal begins an attempt but does not increment the count. Selecting a second card completes the attempt; a mismatch stays visible briefly before both cards turn face down.

What the number can tell you

The theoretical minimum is eight attempts—one for each pair—if every matching location were already known. Early mismatches are part of discovering the board. A useful question after each attempt is what two symbols and locations you learned and whether you can use that information on the next turn.

The layout is reproducible in the current source: the game initializes a seeded shuffle, and reset restores that same arrangement. A lower count can reflect better recall or a more consistent scan, but the game does not store a personal best to compare automatically.

Current-session count, not a saved score

The move total belongs to the active page state and returns to zero when the board is reset. NoCharge V2 does not write a Memory Match best-move key, upload a record, or provide a score dashboard or game-data clearing control. If you want to compare runs, you would need to note the totals yourself.

There is no countdown or speed bonus. The number describes attempts, not reaction time or a claim about memory training. For a repeatable scan, read A systematic way to scan a Memory Match board.
